cemc-euclid-2019-01a.title: Find one quarter
cemc-euclid-2019-01a.body:
$\frac34$ of a jar is $300$ mL, so $\frac14$ of a jar is $300 \div 3 = 100$ mL.

**Answer: 100 mL**

cemc-euclid-2019-01a.title: Find the whole jar
cemc-euclid-2019-01a.body:
The full jar holds $\frac43 \cdot 300 = 400$ mL, so a quarter of it is $400 \div 4 = 100$ mL.

**Answer: 100 mL**

cemc-euclid-2019-01b.title: Invert the inequalities
cemc-euclid-2019-01b.body:
Since $\frac{24}{a} > 0$, $a > 0$. Then $3 < \frac{24}{a}$ gives $a < 8$, and $\frac{24}{a} < 4$ gives $a > 6$. So $a = 7$; indeed $\frac{24}{7} \approx 3.43$.

**Answer: 7**

cemc-euclid-2019-01b.title: Test values
cemc-euclid-2019-01b.body:
$a$ must be positive. $\frac{24}{6} = 4$ (too big — not strictly less than $4$), $\frac{24}{7} \approx 3.43$ ✓, $\frac{24}{8} = 3$ (too small). Larger $a$ give values below $3$ and smaller $a$ give values above $4$.

**Answer: 7**

cemc-euclid-2019-01c.title: Substitute u = 1/x
cemc-euclid-2019-01c.body:
Let $u = \frac1x$. Then $u^2 - u - 2 = 0$, so $(u - 2)(u + 1) = 0$, giving $u = 2$ or $u = -1$, i.e. $x = \frac12$ or $x = -1$.

**Answer: $x = \frac12$ or $x = -1$**

cemc-euclid-2019-02a.title: Subtract the small circles
cemc-euclid-2019-02a.body:
Large circle: $\pi\cdot 2^2 = 4\pi$. Each small circle: $\pi$. The small circles lie inside the large one without overlapping, so the shaded area is $4\pi - 2\pi = 2\pi$.

**Answer: $2\pi$**

cemc-euclid-2019-02a.title: Ratio of areas
cemc-euclid-2019-02a.body:
Each small circle has half the radius of the large circle, hence $\frac14$ of its area. Two of them cover $\frac12$ of the large circle, leaving $\frac12 \cdot 4\pi = 2\pi$ shaded.

**Answer: $2\pi$**

cemc-euclid-2019-02b.title: Find the distance
cemc-euclid-2019-02b.body:
Mo jogs for $1$ hour at $6$ km/h, so the route is $6$ km. Kari needs $\frac{6}{8} = \frac34$ h $= 45$ minutes. Finishing at 11:00, Kari started at 10:15 a.m.

**Answer: 10:15 a.m.**

cemc-euclid-2019-02b.title: Compare times by speed ratio
cemc-euclid-2019-02b.body:
Over the same distance, time is inversely proportional to speed. Kari is $\frac86 = \frac43$ times as fast, so takes $\frac34$ of Mo's $60$ minutes, i.e. $45$ minutes. So Kari started $45$ minutes before 11:00, at 10:15 a.m.

**Answer: 10:15 a.m.**

cemc-euclid-2019-02c.title: Match slopes
cemc-euclid-2019-02c.body:
$x + 3y = 7$ gives $y = -\frac13 x + \frac73$, slope $-\frac13$. Parallel lines have equal slopes, so $m = -\frac13$. Through $(9,2)$: $2 = -\frac13\cdot 9 + b = -3 + b$, so $b = 5$.

**Answer: $b = 5$**

cemc-euclid-2019-02c.title: Parallel line in the same form
cemc-euclid-2019-02c.body:
Lines parallel to $x + 3y = 7$ have equations $x + 3y = c$. Through $(9, 2)$: $c = 9 + 6 = 15$. So the line is $x + 3y = 15$, i.e. $y = -\frac13 x + 5$, and $b = 5$.

**Answer: $b = 5$**

cemc-euclid-2019-03a.title: Compare sums
cemc-euclid-2019-03a.body:
The sum is $168$, so Michelle's average is $168/8 = 21$. Daphne's $7$ numbers average $20$, so their sum is $140$. The removed number is $168 - 140 = 28$.

**Answer: 28**

cemc-euclid-2019-03a.title: Deviation from the mean
cemc-euclid-2019-03a.body:
If the removed number is $r$, the new average is $\frac{168 - r}{7}$. Setting this equal to $20$: $168 - r = 140$, $r = 28$. (Equivalently, removing a number $7$ above the old mean $21$ lowers the mean of the remaining $7$ numbers by $\frac{7}{7} = 1$.)

**Answer: 28**

cemc-euclid-2019-04a.title: Isosceles triangle
cemc-euclid-2019-04a.body:
In right $\triangle CDB$, $\angle DCB = 30^\circ$, so it is a $30$-$60$-$90$ triangle and $CD = 2\cdot DB = 20$.

$\angle ADC = 180^\circ - 60^\circ = 120^\circ$, so $\angle DAC = 180^\circ - 120^\circ - 30^\circ = 30^\circ = \angle ACD$. Triangle $ADC$ is isosceles with $AD = CD = 20$.

**Answer: 20**

cemc-euclid-2019-04a.title: Two 30-60-90 triangles
cemc-euclid-2019-04a.body:
$\angle DCB = 30^\circ$, so $\angle ACB = 60^\circ$ and $\angle CAB = 30^\circ$. From $\triangle CDB$: $CB = 10\sqrt3$. From $\triangle ACB$: $AB = \sqrt3\cdot CB = 30$. So $AD = 30 - 10 = 20$.

**Answer: 20**

cemc-euclid-2019-04b.title: Perpendicular bisector
cemc-euclid-2019-04b.body:
The centre $O$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of $AB$ exactly when $\vec{OM}\cdot\vec{AB} = 0$, where $M$ is the midpoint of $AB$. Here $\vec{AB} = (12 - 2d,\ 3d - 6)$ and $M = (6,\ \frac{d - 6}{2})$:
$$6(12 - 2d) + \tfrac{d-6}{2}(3d - 6) = 0 \iff 144 - 24d + 3d^2 - 24d + 36 = 0 \iff d^2 - 16d + 60 = 0.$$
(If $A = B$ the condition is automatic, but $A = B$ would need $d = 12 - d$ and $-d = 2d - 6$, i.e. $d = 6$ and $d = 2$, impossible.) So $d = 6$ or $d = 10$.

**Answer: $d = 6$ or $d = 10$**

cemc-euclid-2019-05a.title: Square both sides
cemc-euclid-2019-05a.body:
$\sqrt b = \sqrt{50} - \sqrt a$ gives $b = 50 + a - 2\sqrt{50a}$, so $\sqrt{50a} = 5\sqrt{2a}$ must be rational, i.e. $2a$ is a perfect square: $a = 2m^2$. Then $\sqrt a = m\sqrt2$ and $\sqrt b = (5 - m)\sqrt2$, $b = 2(5 - m)^2$. With $0 < a < b$: $m = 1$ or $2$, giving $(2, 32)$ and $(8, 18)$.

**Answer: $(2, 32)$ and $(8, 18)$**

cemc-euclid-2019-05b.title: Reduce to divisors
cemc-euclid-2019-05b.body:
$d \ne 0$ and $c = kd$, so $(k + 1)d = 2000$. Since $k + 1 \ge 1$, an integer solution exists exactly when $k + 1$ divides $2000$ (then $d = \frac{2000}{k+1}$ and $c = 2000 - d$ are integers).

$2000 = 2^4\cdot 5^3$ has $(4+1)(3+1) = 20$ positive divisors, so there are $20$ values of $k$.

**Answer: 20**

cemc-euclid-2019-05b.title: List them
cemc-euclid-2019-05b.body:
The positive divisors of $2000$ are
$1, 2, 4, 5, 8, 10, 16, 20, 25, 40, 50, 80, 100, 125, 200, 250, 400, 500, 1000, 2000$,
twenty in all; each gives $k = (\text{divisor}) - 1 \ge 0$. For example $k + 1 = 8$ gives $k = 7$ with $(c, d) = (1750, 250)$.

**Answer: 20**

cemc-euclid-2019-06a.title: Angle sum of the visible polygon
cemc-euclid-2019-06a.body:
Each angle of the regular pentagon is $108^\circ$; each angle of the $n$-gon is $\frac{n-2}{n}\cdot180^\circ$.

The visible part of the $n$-gon (outside the pentagon) is a heptagon whose angles are: four angles of the $n$-gon, the angles $a^\circ$ and $b^\circ$, and the reflex angle $360^\circ - 108^\circ = 252^\circ$ at the pentagon's vertex. Its angle sum is $5\cdot180^\circ = 900^\circ$:
$$4\cdot\frac{n-2}{n}\cdot180 + 88 + 252 = 900 \implies \frac{n-2}{n} = \frac{560}{720} = \frac79 \implies n = 9.$$

**Answer: $n = 9$**

cemc-euclid-2019-06a.title: Hexagon and triangle
cemc-euclid-2019-06a.body:
Join the two vertices of the $n$-gon at which the angles $a^\circ$ and $b^\circ$ sit. This forms a hexagon (four full angles of the $n$-gon plus angles $a + c$ and $b + d$) and a small triangle with angles $c$, $d$ and the pentagon's $108^\circ$, so $c + d = 72^\circ$.

Hexagon angle sum $720^\circ$: $4\cdot\frac{n-2}{n}\cdot180 + 88 + 72 = 720$, so $\frac{n-2}{n}\cdot 180 = 140$, giving each angle $140^\circ$ and $n = \frac{360}{40} = 9$.

**Answer: $n = 9$**

cemc-euclid-2019-06b.title: Coordinates
cemc-euclid-2019-06b.body:
Let $AD = a$, $AB = ar$, $BC = ar^2$ with $a, r > 0$. The angles at $A$ and $B$ are right angles, so place $B = (0,0)$, $C = (ar^2, 0)$, $A = (0, ar)$, $D = (a, ar)$.

Slope of $BD = \frac{ar}{a} = r$; slope of $AC = \frac{ar - 0}{0 - ar^2} = -\frac1r$. Their product is $-1$, so $AC \perp BD$. ∎

cemc-euclid-2019-06b.title: Similar right triangles
cemc-euclid-2019-06b.body:
Right triangles $DAB$ (right angle at $A$) and $ABC$ (right angle at $B$) have legs in the same ratio: $\frac{AD}{AB} = \frac{AB}{BC}$ (geometric sequence). By SAS similarity, $\triangle DAB \sim \triangle ABC$, so $\angle ABD = \angle BCA$.

Let $P$ be the intersection of $AC$ and $BD$. In $\triangle PBC$: $\angle PBC = 90^\circ - \angle ABD$ and $\angle PCB = \angle BCA = \angle ABD$. So $\angle BPC = 180^\circ - (90^\circ - \angle ABD) - \angle ABD = 90^\circ$. ∎

cemc-euclid-2019-07a.title: Combine logarithms
cemc-euclid-2019-07a.body:
Need $x > 1$. The equation becomes $\log_2\!\left((x-1)^2(x+2)\right) = 1$, so $(x-1)^2(x+2) = 2$, i.e. $x^3 - 3x + 2 = 2$, $x(x^2 - 3) = 0$. Only $x = \sqrt3$ satisfies $x > 1$.

**Answer: $x = \sqrt3$**

cemc-euclid-2019-07a.title: Exponentiate
cemc-euclid-2019-07a.body:
For $x > 1$, raise $2$ to both sides: $2^{2\log_2(x-1)} = (x-1)^2$ and $2^{1 - \log_2(x+2)} = \frac{2}{x+2}$. So $(x-1)^2(x+2) = 2$, which as before gives $x \in \{0, \pm\sqrt3\}$; with $x > 1$ only $x = \sqrt3$ remains, and it works since every step is reversible for $x > 1$.

**Answer: $x = \sqrt3$**

cemc-euclid-2019-07b.title: Peel off one f at a time
Complete the square
cemc-euclid-2019-07b.body:
$f(x) = (x-1)^2 - 1$. Let $u = (x-1)^2 \ge 0$. Then $f(x) = u - 1$, $f(f(x)) = (u-2)^2 - 1$, $f(f(f(x))) = \left((u-2)^2 - 2\right)^2 - 1 = 3$.

So $(u-2)^2 - 2 = \pm 2$: either $(u-2)^2 = 4$ giving $u = 0$ or $u = 4$, or $(u-2)^2 = 0$ giving $u = 2$.

$u = 0 \Rightarrow x = 1$; $u = 4 \Rightarrow x = 3, -1$; $u = 2 \Rightarrow x = 1 \pm\sqrt2$.

**Answer: $x = 3, 1, -1, 1+\sqrt2, 1-\sqrt2$**

cemc-euclid-2019-08a.title: Similar triangles
cemc-euclid-2019-08a.body:
The four equal angles around $O$ are each $90^\circ$. Radii to the tangent points are perpendicular to the sides. In right $\triangle OTA$: $AT = \sqrt{9 - 1} = 2\sqrt2$.

Since $\angle DOA = 90^\circ$ and $OT \perp AD$, $OT$ is the altitude to the hypotenuse of right $\triangle AOD$, so $\triangle ATO \sim \triangle OTD$ and $OT^2 = AT\cdot TD$:
$$TD = \frac{1}{2\sqrt2} = \frac{\sqrt2}{4}.$$
Tangent lengths from $D$ are equal, so $DS = DT = \frac{\sqrt2}{4}$.

**Answer: $DS = \frac{\sqrt2}{4}$**

cemc-euclid-2019-08a.title: Angles
cemc-euclid-2019-08a.body:
In right $\triangle OTA$, $\angle AOT = \alpha$ with $\cos\alpha = \frac13$. Since $\angle AOD = 90^\circ$, $\angle TOD = 90^\circ - \alpha$, and in right $\triangle OTD$: $TD = OT\tan(90^\circ - \alpha) = \cot\alpha = \frac{\cos\alpha}{\sin\alpha} = \frac{1/3}{2\sqrt2/3} = \frac{1}{2\sqrt2}$.

Hence $DS = DT = \frac{\sqrt2}{4}$.

**Answer: $DS = \frac{\sqrt2}{4}$**

cemc-euclid-2019-08b.title: Complementary angles
cemc-euclid-2019-08b.body:
For $0 < x < \frac\pi2$, both $\frac32\cos x$ and $\frac32\sin x$ lie in $(0, \frac32) \subset (0, \frac\pi2)$. For angles $Y, Z$ in $(0, \frac\pi2)$, $\cos Y = \sin Z = \cos(\frac\pi2 - Z)$ holds exactly when $Y = \frac\pi2 - Z$ (cosine is one-to-one there). So
$$\tfrac32\cos x + \tfrac32\sin x = \tfrac\pi2 \iff \sin x + \cos x = \tfrac\pi3.$$
Squaring: $1 + \sin 2x = \frac{\pi^2}{9}$, so $\sin 2x = \frac{\pi^2 - 9}{9}$.

(Such $x$ exists: $\sin x + \cos x$ takes all values in $(1, \sqrt2]$ on $(0, \frac\pi2)$, and $1 < \frac\pi3 < \sqrt2$.)

**Answer: $\sin 2x = \dfrac{\pi^2 - 9}{9}$**

cemc-euclid-2019-08b.title: Sum-to-product
cemc-euclid-2019-08b.body:
Write $\sin(\frac32\sin x) = \cos(\frac\pi2 - \frac32\sin x)$. Then
$$\cos A - \cos B = -2\sin\tfrac{A+B}{2}\sin\tfrac{A-B}{2} = 0$$
with $A = \frac32\cos x$, $B = \frac\pi2 - \frac32\sin x$. Both $A$ and $B$ lie in $(0, \frac\pi2)$, so $\frac{A+B}{2} \in (0, \frac\pi2)$ has nonzero sine and $\frac{A-B}{2} \in (-\frac\pi4, \frac\pi4)$ has zero sine only when $A = B$. So $\frac32(\sin x + \cos x) = \frac\pi2$ and, squaring, $\sin 2x = \frac{\pi^2}{9} - 1 = \frac{\pi^2 - 9}{9}$.

**Answer: $\sin 2x = \dfrac{\pi^2 - 9}{9}$**

cemc-euclid-2019-09b.title: Simplify
cemc-euclid-2019-09b.body:
$f(a,a) = 1 + 1 + \frac{1}{a^2} = 2 + \frac1{a^2}$. This is an integer exactly when $\frac{1}{a^2}$ is, i.e. $a^2 = 1$, so $a = 1$ (giving $f(1,1) = 3$).

**Answer: $a = 1$ only**

cemc-euclid-2019-09b.title: Bound
cemc-euclid-2019-09b.body:
For $a \ge 2$, $0 < \frac1{a^2} \le \frac14$, so $2 < f(a,a) < 3$ is not an integer. For $a = 1$, $f(1,1) = 3$.

**Answer: $a = 1$ only**

cemc-euclid-2019-09c.title: Discriminant mod 3
cemc-euclid-2019-09c.body:
Let $k = f(a, b)$ be an integer. Multiplying by $ab$: $a^2 + b^2 + 1 = kab$, i.e. $a^2 - (kb)a + (b^2 + 1) = 0$. As $a$ is an integer root of this quadratic, its discriminant
$$\Delta = k^2b^2 - 4(b^2 + 1) = b^2(k-2)(k+2) - 4$$
is a perfect square.

Suppose $3 \nmid k$. Then $k \equiv 1$ or $2 \pmod 3$, so $3 \mid k + 2$ or $3 \mid k - 2$; either way $3 \mid (k-2)(k+2)$ and $\Delta \equiv -4 \equiv 2 \pmod 3$. But squares are $\equiv 0$ or $1 \pmod 3$ (as $(3q)^2, (3q\pm1)^2 \equiv 0, 1$). Contradiction. Hence $3 \mid k$. ∎

cemc-euclid-2019-09c.title: Squares mod 3 directly
cemc-euclid-2019-09c.body:
From $a^2 + b^2 + 1 = kab$, work mod $3$. Squares are $0$ or $1$ mod $3$.

- If $3 \mid a$: then $b^2 + 1 \equiv 0$, i.e. $b^2 \equiv 2$, impossible. Similarly $3 \nmid b$.
- So $a^2 \equiv b^2 \equiv 1$ and the left side is $\equiv 3 \equiv 0 \pmod 3$. Thus $3 \mid kab$; since $3 \nmid a$ and $3 \nmid b$, $3 \mid k$. ∎

cemc-euclid-2019-09d.title: Vieta jumping
cemc-euclid-2019-09d.body:
$f(a,b) = 3 \iff a^2 + b^2 + 1 = 3ab$. Fix $a$: as a quadratic in $b$, $b^2 - 3ab + (a^2 + 1) = 0$, its two roots sum to $3a$. So if $f(a, b) = 3$ then also $f(b, 3b - a) = 3$ (by symmetry, apply this with the roles swapped). Directly:
$$b^2 + (3b-a)^2 + 1 - 3b(3b - a) = a^2 + b^2 - 3ab + 1 = 0.$$
Starting from $f(1,2) = 3$:
$(2, 5) \to (5, 13) \to (13, 34) \to (34, 89) \to (89, 233)$.

Check e.g. $f(5,13) = \frac{25 + 169 + 1}{65} = \frac{195}{65} = 3$.

**Answer (one possibility): $(5,13), (13,34), (34,89), (89,233)$**

cemc-euclid-2019-10a.title: Amir wins on turn 2 or 3
cemc-euclid-2019-10a.body:
Brigitte has only two colours, so she wins by her third turn at the latest. Hence Amir can only win on his 2nd or 3rd turn.

- Win on 2nd turn: his second card matches his first: $\frac15$.
- Win on 3rd turn: his 2nd card doesn't match ($\frac45$), Brigitte's 2nd card doesn't match hers ($\frac23$), and his 3rd card matches one of his first two ($\frac24$): $\frac45\cdot\frac23\cdot\frac12 = \frac4{15}$.

Total: $\frac15 + \frac4{15} = \frac7{15}$.

**Answer: $\frac7{15}$**

cemc-euclid-2019-10a.title: Complement
cemc-euclid-2019-10a.body:
Amir loses if he hasn't won by the time Brigitte gets a pair. Brigitte wins on her 2nd turn with probability $\frac13$ (her 2nd card matches), on her 3rd turn otherwise (certainly).

$P(\text{Amir loses}) = P(\text{no Amir pair after 2})\cdot\left[\tfrac13 + \tfrac23\cdot P(\text{no Amir pair on 3rd} )\right] = \frac45\left[\frac13 + \frac23\cdot\frac12\right] = \frac45\cdot\frac23 = \frac8{15}$.

So $P(\text{Amir wins}) = 1 - \frac8{15} = \frac7{15}$.

**Answer: $\frac7{15}$**

cemc-euclid-2019-10b.title: Peel off one coin at a time
cemc-euclid-2019-10b.body:
**Yes.** Let $p$ be the probability of an even number of heads among the first $13$ coins. Then
$$\tfrac12 = p(1 - h_{14}) + (1 - p)h_{14} \iff 0 = (2p - 1)(2h_{14} - 1).$$
So $h_{14} = \frac12$ or $p = \frac12$. In the second case, repeat the argument with $13$ coins, and so on. Either some $h_k = \frac12$ for $k \ge 2$, or eventually the probability of an even number of heads with coin $1$ alone is $\frac12$, i.e. $1 - h_1 = \frac12$ and $h_1 = \frac12$. ∎

cemc-euclid-2019-10b.title: Product formula
cemc-euclid-2019-10b.body:
**Yes.** Let $E$ and $O$ be the probabilities of an even/odd number of heads. Expanding $\prod_{k=1}^{14}\left((1 - h_k) + h_k t\right)$, the coefficient of $t^j$ is the probability of exactly $j$ heads. Setting $t = -1$:
$$E - O = \prod_{k=1}^{14}(1 - 2h_k).$$
$E = \frac12$ means $E - O = 0$, so some factor $1 - 2h_k = 0$, i.e. $h_k = \frac12$. ∎

cemc-euclid-2019-10c.title: Factor S(7) − S(2) − S(12)
cemc-euclid-2019-10c.body:
$S(2) = p_1q_1$, $S(12) = p_6q_6$, $S(7) = p_1q_6 + p_2q_5 + p_3q_4 + p_4q_3 + p_5q_2 + p_6q_1$.

Since $S(2) = S(12) = \frac12 S(7) > 0$: $p_1q_1 = p_6q_6$ and $p_1, q_1, p_6, q_6 > 0$. If $p_1 = p_6$ then dividing gives $q_1 = q_6$ (and vice versa), so it suffices to show $p_1 = p_6$.

From $S(7) - S(2) - S(12) = 0$:
$$p_1q_6 + p_6q_1 - p_1q_1 - p_6q_6 + (p_2q_5 + p_3q_4 + p_4q_3 + p_5q_2) = 0,$$
$$(p_1 - p_6)(q_1 - q_6) = p_2q_5 + p_3q_4 + p_4q_3 + p_5q_2 \ge 0.$$
Suppose $p_1 > p_6$. Then $q_1 \ge q_6$, so $p_1q_1 > p_6q_6$ — contradiction. Suppose $p_1 < p_6$. Then $q_1 \le q_6$, so $p_1q_1 < p_6q_6$ — contradiction. Hence $p_1 = p_6$, and then $q_1 = q_6$. ∎

cemc-euclid-2019-10c.title: AM-GM
cemc-euclid-2019-10c.body:
With $S(2) = p_1q_1 = p_6q_6 = s > 0$ and $S(7) = 2s$:
$$2s = S(7) \ge p_1q_6 + p_6q_1.$$
By AM-GM, $p_1q_6 + p_6q_1 \ge 2\sqrt{p_1q_6p_6q_1} = 2\sqrt{s\cdot s} = 2s$. So equality holds throughout; equality in AM-GM requires $p_1q_6 = p_6q_1$. Combined with $p_1q_1 = p_6q_6$: dividing, $\frac{q_6}{q_1} = \frac{q_1}{q_6}$, so $q_1 = q_6$ (both positive), and then $p_1 = p_6$. ∎
